output.headline: Fonagy review sets out scale of ADHD and autism demand facing NHS
output.bodyHtml:
The NHS in England should move to a “needs-led” system for mental health, ADHD and autism care, a government-commissioned review has concluded, after finding that the health service is heading into a “world of system failures” as it struggles to cope with demand that has left more than 800,000 people waiting for an ADHD or autism assessment, some of them desperate for support.

The review said patients’ needs meant the NHS should bring together mental health and neurodevelopmental services and move to a “needs-led” system.

The Royal College of Paediatrics and Child Health backed Fonagy’s call for diagnosis to no longer dictate who receives care.

Dr Ronny Cheung, the college’s officer for health services, said: “Too often, a diagnosis is the only route to accessing meaningful help. This means that children and families can be left struggling alone while waiting for assessments, with little or no support available in the meantime.”

Moving to a “needs-led” approach would “ensure children and young people can seamlessly and more quickly access a robust, holistic and reliable standard of care”, he added.

Yvette Cooper, the health secretary, will draw on Fonagy’s recommendations as she puts together the forthcoming mental health strategy, due by the end of the year.

In her response, Cooper promised that the NHS would provide a “needs-led” system under which people would get much faster care, and she has asked NHS England to establish how it can provide faster advice, assessments and treatment.

She said: “It is clear that mental health services need to change to focus more on the early support young people need to stay in education or work or keep their lives on track.”

She also pledged to ensure all private assessment clinics are regulated, though she did not commit to the advertising ban Fonagy said was needed.

Prof Peter Fonagy led the review, which examined the sharp rise in demand over recent decades for help with mental health and neurodevelopmental conditions and produced the warning of system failures.

It urged ministers to toughen regulation of the private clinics that many people turn to because they cannot get assessed quickly by the NHS, while warning of an increasing risk of overdiagnosis of autism and attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD).

The experts behind the review also called for access to care to be based primarily on a person’s needs so fewer people would have years-long waits for a formal diagnosis.

Related: NHS England mental health services review: what has it found and what does it recommend?

The review found that the number of people suffering mental distress has risen significantly across all age groups in England since the 1990s, especially the under-18s.

The number of 16- to 64-year-olds with a common mental disorder increased from 15.5 per cent in 1993 to 22.6 per cent in 2024. However, it jumped more sharply – from about one in six to one in four – among 16- to 24-year-olds over the same period.

The report, which runs to 607 pages, found that the evidence shows sceptics are wrong to cast doubt on young people’s struggles.

“That’s sometimes been attributed to personal failures, people being told they’re making it up, it’s all in their head, which is absolute nonsense,” said Prof Simon Wessely, a leading psychiatrist and vice-chair of the review.

The findings may have significant implications for the government’s drive to reduce the number of young people in the UK not in education, employment or training – now almost 1 million – and the size of the welfare bill, with a record 2.8 million people too sick to work; and also for schools as they grapple with the demands arising from the growing number of pupils with special educational needs.

Fonagy, a psychoanalyst and clinical psychologist at University College London, dismissed the notion that young people in particular were “snowflakes” who were less resilient than in previous generations. “The rise in mental health problems is real, is affecting everyday functioning and cannot be explained by greater awareness alone,” his report said.

He said an array of social and economic circumstances had piled unprecedented pressure on young people. “There is increased uncertainty – financial pressures, insecure work, unaffordable housing – but perhaps more important, a lack of hope among young people that their lives will be better than their parents, and that’s the first time since the second world war that surveys have noticed that.”

Fonagy said the explosion in demand for help with mental ill-health and neurodiversity had left people stuck on waiting lists for years at a time and with worsening symptoms. At the end of last year more than 560,000 people in England were waiting to be assessed for ADHD – 17 times more than in 2019 – and another 254,000 were waiting for a diagnostic assessment for autism, taking the total waiting to more than 800,000, almost all of them – 90 per cent – for at least three months.

The number of six- to 11-year-olds diagnosed with autism has also soared, jumping 20-fold to 4.58 per cent between 2000 and 2025, and by even more among those aged 12 to 17 over the same years – from 0.1 per cent to 4.06 per cent, a 40-fold rise. The proportion of six- to 11-year-olds with an ADHD diagnosis has increased more than sixfold in five years, and more than 15-fold among 12- to 17-year-olds, to 2.7 per cent and 3.9 per cent respectively.

The report warned that if current trends continue, the 4 million children who already suffer “high psychological distress” could become 4.5 million by 2030, with the number of under-18s who self-harm rising from 1.9 million to 2.5 million.

Wessely warned that the exponential rise in diagnoses of autism and ADHD means the UK has reached a “tipping point” where people are at risk of being misdiagnosed with either condition.

The authors did not find that overdiagnosis was occurring at scale, but added that the evidence “suggests we are entering a phase in which the balance of risks between underdiagnosis, misdiagnosis and overdiagnosis may be changing, with the risks of misdiagnosis and overdiagnosis becoming increasingly important considerations for policy and service delivery”.

The increasing tendency of young people to self-identify as neurodivergent – as many as a fifth of secondary school pupils do so – means that “the line between the social and the medical is beginning to blur”, they added.

The 10-month review found “strong concerns about the consistency and quality of ADHD and autism assessments being carried out by independent providers, and the financial incentives associated with assessment activity”.

Ministers should ban direct-to-public advertising of such services and ensure that all clinics offering them are regulated by the Care Quality Commission, it said.

Growing numbers of young people have a combination of mental ill-health and ADHD or autism, or both. “Co-occurence is the rule rather than the exception,” the report said. For example, 61 per cent of 16- to 24-year-olds with a common mental health condition also had autistic traits, and 57 per cent had ADHD symptoms.
output.standfirst: A government-commissioned review by Prof Peter Fonagy sets out the scale of demand for ADHD, autism and mental health care, after finding the NHS risks ‘system failures’ with more than 800,000 people waiting for assessment.
output.progress: Yvette Cooper has asked NHS England to find ways to provide faster assessments and treatment, drawing on the review for her mental health strategy.

output.headline: Three sisters spent final hours together before taking their own lives in Brighton
output.bodyHtml:
Jane Adetoro and her younger sisters, Christina and Rebecca Walters, were “the closest sisters and the best friends”, according to their family. Devoted to their father, Joseph, whom they messaged every day, the adult siblings lived quiet lives in the flat they shared in west London and would do everything together.

When they died in May this year, it was no different. Early in the morning of 13 May, the sisters’ bodies were recovered from the sea in Brighton, hours after a taxi had dropped the three women at the beachfront.

On Thursday, an inquest in the city found that the women, who all drowned, died by suicide a day after making a pilgrimage together to the lake in Birmingham where their mother died by drowning 16 years earlier.

In a statement, Joseph Jacobson told the inquest that the scale of his loss was indescribable. “There are no words that can adequately express the pain of losing a child. To lose all three of my precious daughters, Jane, Christina and Rebecca, is a heartbreak beyond anything I could ever have imagined.”

Jacobson, who attended the inquest by video link, said he could not understand why their lives had ended so suddenly. “You were my daughters, you will always be my daughters and I will love you for the rest of my life. May your beautiful souls rest in perfect peace,” he said.

Precisely why Jane, 36, Christina, known as Tina, 32, and 31-year-old Rebecca, or Becky, decided to end their lives may never be known, the senior coroner Penelope Schofield told the hearing at Woodvale coroner’s court in Brighton.

“These three sisters lived very secluded lives. They were incredibly private. We don’t know why they took this course of action or indeed why they chose to do it in Brighton,” Schofield said.

What police were able to establish, after initial public bafflement over the circumstances of the tragedy, is how the women spent the day before they died. On the night of 11 May, the sisters travelled by Uber from their home in Greenford, west London, to Birmingham, where they were dropped off at 11.36pm in Linton Walk, in the north of the city.

This was the address where Jane and Rebecca, then 20 and 15, were living with their mother, Janice Adetoro, when she disappeared on 5 January 2010, prompting an anguished public appeal by family members. (Christina, then 16, was reportedly living with her father at the time.) Janice’s body was recovered a month later from Brookvale Park Lake, which runs to the end of Linton Walk. She was 43.

Described as a doting mother, Janice had been suffering from “paranoid delusions”, the inquest into her death heard. She was sectioned and admitted to a psychiatric unit, the Sunday Times reported, but was discharged from a home treatment team weeks before her death.

The tragedy of the sisters’ deaths “wasn’t a story that started in May”, their cousin Natalie Walters-Daniel told the newspaper last month. “It was a story that started long before.”

DCI Mark Cullimore, of Sussex police, told the inquest there was no CCTV to show what the three sisters did in the time they were in Birmingham, but less than two hours after arriving, at 1.28am on 12 May, they were picked up by taxi and driven back to their London flat.

The inquest heard that Christina, who had recently graduated from Brunel University of London and worked as an accountant, had experienced anxiety and depression since her mother’s death and made “extensive searches” about suicide in the days before her own death.

Jane, who was also an accountant, had paid off a loan in full on 11 May. Described as “extremely intelligent”, Jane was said by family members to have taken on a maternal role after the death of her own mother.

Rebecca, “the baby” to relatives, worked in HR. She was previously described as “mischievous” and “the lively one who was always cracking jokes”.

The two younger sisters had changed their names to their mother’s maiden name after her death. “Their mother’s death was a hard thing to carry and bear,” their cousin said. “They held a certain level of their feelings to themselves … I believe it was their own coping mechanism.”

On the evening on 12 May, the inquest heard, the three women caught a train to Brighton, arriving at 10.20pm, and then took a car to the beachfront near the marina. The Uber driver was struck by the lack of conversation between them, he later told police.

Sussex police reviewed hundreds of hours of CCTV to establish that for at least four hours the women paced the seafront in the darkness. They were picked up periodically in snatches of footage, last being seen at 2.42am. It was a windy night and the sea was particularly rough, Cullimore told the inquest.

Emergency services were called after a cyclist reported seeing a body on the beach shortly before 5.45am. Jane was brought to shore by an RNLI crew and declared dead at the scene. Christina’s body was also located by the lifeboat crew. Rebecca’s body was recovered from Brighton beach where it appeared to have been washed to shore. None of the women had been able to swim.

Cullimore told the inquest he had “remained open-minded throughout and always considered whether there was third-party involvement” but he was now satisfied there had not been. There was no evidence that any of the sisters had used drugs or alcohol, and no indication of any violence.

The coroner found that all three had intended to die. “I will record in respect for each of them that on 12 May they entered the sea at West Beach, Brighton, to end their lives,” she said. “They could not swim and the conditions were adverse.”

  • In the UK and Ireland, Samaritans can be contacted on freephone 116 123. In the US, you can call or text the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline at 988 or chat at 988lifeline.org. In Australia, the crisis support service Lifeline is 13 11 14. Other international helplines can be found at befrienders.org
output.standfirst: An inquest in Brighton heard how Jane Adetoro and her sisters Christina and Rebecca Walters spent their final days together; the coroner said why they ended their lives may never be known.

output.headline: Mountbatten-Windsor wins legal challenge against Thames Valley police
output.bodyHtml:
Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor has won his legal challenge against Thames Valley police over the search warrants used to raid his home after his arrest.

On Thursday, Mr Justice Hilliard, sitting at the high court in central London, ruled that the search warrants were unlawful, after Thames Valley police (TVP) conceded it had obtained the search powers under the wrong statutory provision.

The former prince had brought a judicial review of the legality of the force’s actions and those of the central criminal court, which had granted the warrants.

Police believe the ruling will not affect the success of the investigation, though the episode is embarrassing for TVP.

The warrants were issued by an Old Bailey judge on 18 February and Mountbatten-Windsor was subsequently arrested the following day, on his 66th birthday, on suspicion of misconduct in public office.

The arrest followed information that emerged from the Jeffrey Epstein files. It was alleged that when Mountbatten-Windsor was the UK’s trade envoy he shared sensitive information with Epstein, a convicted child sex offender.

Police began searching the former Duke of York’s residence on the Sandringham estate and his former Windsor home, Royal Lodge, on the same day as his arrest. Documentary material and electronic devices were seized.

Hilliard said the search warrants were quashed, though police had made an application, to be heard next year, to retain the seized property on the basis that it would have been lawful to take it under a different statutory provision. Mountbatten-Windsor opposes that application.

The judge said: “The fact that the search warrants were quashed does not bring the investigation to an end or mean that the whole of the investigation is unlawful.”

A senior police source said: “It’s not going to bring the investigation to a halt or affect the chances of success.”

They added: “The news media might say the police messed up. But it was the judicial decision [to grant the warrant] that was incorrect.”

TVP have been in discussions with lawyers from the Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) about the strength of their case and what evidence they would need for a prosecution.

A TVP spokesperson said: “The agreement that led to the quashing of the warrants relates specifically to a decision made by the court regarding the legal basis for these and is not a judgment on our ongoing investigation.

“We ensured the court was presented with all the necessary information and paperwork to inform their decision, following the correct legal processes throughout.

“We accept the position that the initial court’s decision to issue warrants under the specific piece of legislation used was incorrect and therefore these must be legally quashed.”

Hilliard told the court that the grant of a search warrant under section eight of the Police and Criminal Evidence Act (Pace) 1984 was conditional on the issuing judge being satisfied there were reasonable grounds to suspect that the material sought did not include items subject to legal privilege or special procedure material.

Special procedure material includes documents in possession of a person who acquired them in the course of any trade, business, profession or other occupation – for the purpose of any paid or unpaid office – who holds it subject to an express or implied undertaking to hold it in confidence.

The judge said the presence of legally privileged material was expressly envisaged in the application for the search warrants and that material was likely to be in the possession of Mountbatten-Windsor “who had acquired or created it in circumstances which would make it special procedure material”. He concluded that a lawful warrant could only have been issued under section nine of Pace.

Nick Vamos, the former head of special crime at the CPS, said: “Given the technical nature of the errors revealed today, I expect the crown court to rule in due course that the police can keep the material, or at least as much of it as they would have been entitled to seize in the first place, so they may not ultimately pay much of a price beyond today’s red faces.”

Late last year, King Charles stripped his brother of his right to be a prince and of his dukedom over his association with Epstein.

Mountbatten-Windsor receives an annual stipend, the amount of which has not been disclosed, from King Charles’s private funds, but a palace source told reporters it had been made clear this should not be used to fund the judicial review.
output.standfirst: Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor has won a high court challenge, after police admitted using the wrong legal power to search his homes; the ruling is embarrassing but unlikely to affect their investigation.
output.progress: Thames Valley police are discussing the case with the CPS and will ask a court next year to keep the seized material.

output.headline: Fort Hood shooter Nidal Hasan to be executed by firing squad
output.bodyHtml:
Hasan opened fire at a medical processing center on the Texas base on 5 November 2009, killing 13 people and wounding dozens more. A military jury sentenced him to death in 2013, and he has been held at Fort Leavenworth in Kansas ever since. He exhausted his appeals last year, which cleared the way for Donald Trump to approve the sentence this week on a recommendation from Hegseth.

Pete Hegseth has said the execution of Nidal Hasan, the former army psychiatrist who killed 13 people at Fort Hood, will be a public event when the sentence is carried out later this year. A defense department official later confirmed the execution will be livestreamed.

In an interview with Real America’s Voice, the Pentagon secretary said the firing squad will carry out the sentence at Fort Hood, Texas, at 1pm on Thursday, 3 December. This would be the first US military execution in more than 60 years.

“It was a radical Islamist attack in uniform inside the ranks, and so he’s going to get a firing squad of soldiers, as it should be, and we’ll make sure that people are able to watch it, that it’s public, because people need to understand there’s serious consequences for these types of things,” Hegseth said.

Investigators had found that Hasan had exchanged 18 emails with Anwar al-Awlaki, a radical cleric who was subsequently killed in a US drone strike, in the months before the attack. At his court martial, Hasan said he had acted to stop American soldiers from deploying to Afghanistan to kill fellow Muslims, before his own impending deployment. A review led by William Webster, a former FBI director, concluded that the bureau should have investigated his correspondence more thoroughly.

In the interview, Hegseth said Barack Obama had called the attack “workplace violence”. The Pentagon initially treated the shooting as a workplace-violence incident rather than a terrorist attack, a classification that affected the victims’ eligibility for Purple Hearts and other combat-related benefits.

But there is no record of Obama himself using the phrase. At a memorial days after the attack, he instead described the victims as Americans who had been unable to escape “the horror of war”, while calling the shooting a tragedy and saying the killer would face justice.

The last known case of a military firing squad in the US was in November 1945, but the Trump administration has sought to bring it back in Trump’s second term to expedite capital punishment cases. Five US states allow for firing squads: Idaho, Mississippi, Oklahoma, South Carolina and Utah.

Abroad, Amnesty International’s most recent annual review lists Afghanistan, China, North Korea, Saudi Arabia, Somalia, Taiwan, the United Arab Emirates and Yemen among the countries that still use firing squads.

Asked whether Hasan had made a final request or reached out to Trump, Hegseth replied: “Don’t care. We’ll see him on December 3.”
output.standfirst: Nidal Hasan, the former army psychiatrist who killed 13 people at Fort Hood in 2009, will be executed by firing squad on 3 December, the first US military execution in more than 60 years.

output.headline: Swift security response leads to arrest of two men at Nato base
output.bodyHtml:
Police arrested two Latvian men inside the perimeter of RAF Molesworth in the early hours of Thursday, after they were discovered inside the Cambridgeshire base, which is used by the US military and Nato for intelligence operations.

Military police launched the investigation four hours earlier, after discovering an abandoned vehicle outside the facility, and picked up the men, aged 32 and 36, inside the base at 2am.

Military police, helped by officers from Cambridgeshire police, found a small hole in the perimeter fence before finding and arresting the men, initially on suspicion of trespass on a prohibited site and causing criminal damage.

The suspects, Latvian nationals living in the UK, were then further arrested on suspicion of an offence under section 4 of the National Security Act 2023 – namely entering a prohibited place for a purpose prejudicial to the UK.

The abandoned vehicle was taken to a nearby police location. Initial searches led concerned officers to call in explosives specialists to carry out further checks, though nothing concerning was found.

A police cordon briefly imposed on part of the A1 south of Peterborough and around the village of Glatton, as a precaution, has since been lifted. Officers were carrying out two searches at addresses in the Peterborough area in connection with the investigation, counter-terror police added in a statement.

Both men remained in police custody on Thursday.

Counter-terror police are now leading the investigation because of the nature of the incident, which comes a few days after the US withdrew B-1 bombers from RAF Fairford in Gloucestershire amid concerns about a possible Iran-directed attack.

Commander Helen Flanagan, head of counter-terrorism policing London, said there was nothing at this stage to suggest a connection to September’s incident near RAF Fairford, but said investigators had yet to determine what the men had been doing.

“Our investigation into this incident is at its very early stages. A big part of this is looking at any potential motivation as to why the men were present at the site, but I must stress we are keeping an open mind at this stage and inquiries are very much ongoing,” she added.

Investigators said it was unclear at this stage if there was a hostile state link to the men’s presence on the base, if they were criminals, or whether they had ended up on the site in a misjudged state of late-night exuberance.

RAF Molesworth is home to Nato’s Intelligence Fusion Centre, which provides military intelligence to Nato, and the US Joint Intelligence Operations Center, Europe, which provides a similar service for the US military’s European command, though not Centcom, which is responsible for Iran.

Air Chief Marshal Sir Richard Knighton, the head of the armed forces, said he had “confidence around the safety and security of our bases” as he visited troops on a military exercise in Wales earlier on Thursday.

The chief of defence staff cited the “enormously close relationships from an intelligence perspective and operationally with the US” as reasons for his confidence, but said the US had removed its bombers from Fairford as a precaution.

“The decision to remove the bombers, which don’t ordinarily live there … to take them back was an operational decision to reduce the risk,” he added. The bombers were suddenly redeployed on Sunday, amid reports that the US feared Iran could orchestrate a drone attack on B-1 planes on the ground.

British sources remain sceptical that Iran would have the capability to launch an attack of such sophistication, though the investigation into why five men driving three white vans descended on a village next to Fairford continues.

Mark Rowley, the Met police chief, said the public would “see more progress on this investigation”, and urged them to trust the police as they worked with spy agencies MI5, GCHQ and intelligence partners internationally.

The five men arrested near RAF Fairford, all British nationals in their 20s from London, have been released on police bail without charge, as has a sixth, a dual UK-Iranian national, who was arrested subsequently.

A seventh man, aged 22, who was arrested on Wednesday on suspicion of preparing terrorist acts, was also let out on bail on Thursday.

Rowley acknowledged the threat landscape appeared to have changed. “We’re dealing with an increased tempo of terrorists and also of threats that are directed by foreign states such as Iran and Russia,” he said in a radio interview.
output.standfirst: Military and Cambridgeshire police found a breach in RAF Molesworth's perimeter fence and arrested two Latvian men, 32 and 36, on suspicion of trespass, criminal damage and entering a prohibited place for a prejudicial purpose.
output.progress: Military and Cambridgeshire police tracked the breach, arrested the two men, found nothing concerning in their searches, and lifted the precautionary cordon.

output.headline: French ministers pledge 3,000 substitute teachers after student protests
output.bodyHtml:
Amid the 10th day of nationwide protest, the education minister, Édouard Geffray, told TF1 television on Thursday night that 3,000 substitute teachers would be deployed to about 100 high schools identified as having particularly acute teacher shortages “between tomorrow and Tuesday”.

Geffray said he would also authorise the recruitment of “several hundred” new teachers. The prime minister, Sébastien Lecornu, said the government would propose amendments to the 2027 budget to “translate some of the students’ demands into concrete measures, particularly regarding teacher replacements”.

High school students have again blockaded schools and marched through cities across France, promising to continue their campaign against the poor state of the national education system in the 10th day of protests that have left hundreds injured.

Large crowds took to the streets on Thursday for mainly peaceful demonstrations in cities including Lille, Rennes, Nantes, Lyon, Toulon and Marseille, while in Paris a large procession marched through the city centre to the Place de la Bastille.

An estimated 25,000 students thronged the square in the east of the capital, with some climbing the monument at its centre, which commemorates France’s 1830 July revolution, while waving the tricolour flag and singing the Marseillaise.

As the evening drew in, riot police fired teargas and crowd-dispersal rounds and carried out repeated baton charges to clear the protesters, some of whom hurled bottles, paving stones and other projectiles at the heavily armoured squads.

Eliane, 16, a pupil on the Paris march, said she had come to “defend and encourage high schools in an even worse state than mine”, calling the march “magnificent”. She said she planned to continue protesting until concrete progress was achieved.

Related: ‘This is state violence’: Paris students rage at politicians and heavy-handed policing

Students earlier said the government’s reaction was not sufficient. Ryad Rani, the president of one high school students’ union, said the protesters had heard “no concrete measures whatsoever, no response to our demands”. The movement “will continue”, he said.

Sabrine Kharbach, from another students’ association, said the protest, over teacher shortages, long school hours and dilapidated buildings, would last “for as long as €10bn hasn’t been put on the table”, the amount students and some leftwing politicians have said needs to be urgently invested in France’s schools.

According to an Elabe poll ​for BFM TV, 72% of French people think the students’ demands are legitimate but 55% of them think the protests should stop. Unions called for another national day of action in support of the students next Tuesday.

The education ministry said fewer high schools had been forced to close than in recent days, with 224 shut on Thursday morning and 157 by lunchtime, meaning that about 95% of the country’s high schools were at least partly open.

The interior ministry said more than 71,000 protesters took to the streets on Thursday, in demonstrations backed by many teachers, parents and unions that involved further clashes with police around some school barricades in Paris. In Rennes, riot officers used water cannon to disperse protesters.

A prominent complaint on student banners and placards was the heavy-handed police response to the wave of protests. “Too young to be listened ​to, but old enough to be teargassed,” read one banner on the Paris march.

Over the past two weeks, some demonstrators have set dustbins on fire outside their schools, destroyed bus shelters and hurled projectiles at riot police, who have responded using batons, teargas and riot-control rounds.

At least 215 teenagers, 89 school staff and 761 police officers have been injured since the start of the protests, which were triggered by chronic teacher shortages, crowded classes, dilapidated buildings and long school days.

Related: The Guardian view on the French school protests: the political class needs to heed the voice of students | Editorial

The government on Wednesday suspended the use of stun grenades by police after a teenager’s hand was blown off, while saying it was “excessive” to speak of “police repression” and denying that officers had “orders to confront” the young protesters.

The protests have rocked a government caught between popular demands for investment in deteriorating public services and pressure from markets to reduce France’s ballooning budget deficit and debt mountain, among the highest in the EU.

The economy minister, Roland Lescure, said this week there was room to address demands for more school resources in the 2027 budget. In the current draft, schools have the second-largest funding increase after defence, with a 1.4% hike to €90.9bn.

Six months away from a crucial presidential election to replace Emmanuel Macron, politicians are jockeying to exploit the protests, with the far-right frontrunner, Marine Le Pen, highlighting the damage to schools and calling for parents ⁠to foot repair bills.

Her hard-left opponent, Jean-Luc Mélenchon, has praised the protesters ​as “incredible” and denounced police brutality.
output.standfirst: France's education minister has pledged 3,000 substitute teachers and new recruitment, after 10 days of protests over school conditions left hundreds injured; students say the response is not enough and vow to continue.
output.progress: The government suspended the use of stun grenades by police on Wednesday after a teenager's hand was blown off.

output.headline: Most Japanese now back a woman inheriting the throne, poll finds
output.bodyHtml:
Her face is splashed across magazine covers. Fans flock to online stores to snap up her outfits. At official engagements, huge crowds wait in the crushing heat to catch a glimpse of a woman revered for her ‘regal dignity, beauty and aura’.

Princess Aiko, 24, is the most popular member of Japan’s imperial family, but according to law she will never be empress and, as the country runs out of royals, more and more Japanese people are asking why.

Related: Japan’s second in line to emperor’s throne comes of age amid succession debate

The debate has gathered momentum in the years since Aiko, the only child of Emperor Naruhito and Empress Masako, has transformed from a shy primary school pupil into a young woman at ease with public and media attention.

Japanese citizens support a change, irrespective of their political loyalties. In a poll conducted in April by the Mainichi Shimbun newspaper, 72 per cent favoured the idea of a woman becoming emperor, while just 10 per cent opposed it.

Under a law established almost 140 years ago, women are forbidden from ascending to Japan’s Chrysanthemum throne. But the regulation defies public support for changes that would allow a woman to become empress regnant and avert a looming succession crisis.

The imperial family is facing the same demographic winds buffeting the rest of the country: three decades ago it had 30 members; now there are just 16, only five of them men.

Pressure to change the male-only succession law, passed in 1947 but based on legislation introduced during the Meiji era in 1889, is intensifying, forcing the conservative government of Sanae Takaichi to address the dearth of male heirs to the 1,500-year-old imperial throne.

Just three men comprise the current line of succession – Emperor Naruhito’s younger brother, Crown Prince Akishino; his son, Prince Hisahito; and the emperor’s uncle, Prince Hitachi, who is 90.

If Prince Hisahito, a 20-year-old university student, and the first male born into the imperial family for four decades, does not have a son, the line of succession will come to an end within a generation.

Previous governments have tried to solve the succession question by considering legislation that would finally bring gender equality to the rarefied corridors of the imperial palace in Tokyo. But pressure from conservative MPs – and Hisahito’s birth in 2006 – brought the debate to an abrupt end.

Takaichi triggered anger this summer when her party and its conservative allies pushed through amendments that will safeguard the male-only succession for generations.

The changes, which go into effect later this month, allow women to retain their royal status after marrying non-royals, and resurrects male-line descendants belonging to 11 ‘collateral branches’ of the family that left the imperial fold after the end of the second world war.

In theory, that means a distant male relative could be ‘adopted’ into the heart of the family provided he is single and aged over 15. If he marries and his wife gives birth to a son, that child would then join the line of succession.

The fate of Japan’s imperial family has attracted international attention. In 2024, the UN women’s rights committee urged the Japanese government to allow a female emperor. Tokyo dismissed the intervention as ‘regrettable’ and ‘inappropriate’, saying the imperial succession was a matter of ‘fundamental national identity’.

The UN and Japanese public opinion have crashed against the hard rock of conservative ideology espoused by Takaichi – Japan’s first female prime minister.

During the succession revision debate, she told lawmakers: ‘The unparalleled historic fact that the imperial line has been maintained through the male line for 126 generations is the foundation of the emperor’s authority and legitimacy.’

Takaichi has also said that the revisions were intended only to ease the succession crisis, not to settle the debate over female emperors.

But Prof Makoto Okawa, an expert on imperial lineage and succession at Chuo University in Tokyo, said the recent amendment ‘clearly points towards maintaining the male-line succession’.

Aiko’s popularity could force a rethink, however, given the ‘growing sense of unease among members of the public about excluding someone from the possibility of succeeding to the throne solely because she is a woman’.

‘Many people in Japan have watched Princess Aiko grow up. The composure, dignity and grace she has displayed in recent diplomatic and other official engagements have contributed to the strong public support she enjoys. Many people see her as embodying and carrying forward Emperor Naruhito’s understanding of the role of the emperor as a symbol of the nation who remains close to the people.’

Jin, an Aiko fan who manages an Instagram account devoted to the princess, said the government had ignored the overwhelming consensus behind a change to the male-only succession law.

In her eyes, Aiko is more than qualified to succeed her father.

‘She is the emperor’s only direct descendant, and her character and dignity are of the highest caliber. Aiko is someone who is clearly worthy of serving as a symbol of Japan.’

Aiko – or another future female member of the imperial family – would not be the first female to ascend the throne. Japan has had eight female monarchs, although their role was to sustain the imperial line until a male heir was born. Go-Sakuramachi, who ruled from 1762 to 1770, was the most recent.

Japan’s royals, who are forbidden from commenting on politics, have employed typically nuanced language to communicate their unease with the status quo.

At a press conference in June, the emperor said of the succession debate in parliament: ‘I hope discussions on how to secure the number of imperial family members … gain the understanding of the people.’

His younger brother, Akishino, went further, telling reporters: ‘It is important for society to keep progressing … I believe the duty of the imperial family is to act in response to the requests of society … I do not think there are any differences between women and men.’

output.headline: Plant selfie on Instagram leads scientists to new giant waterlily species
output.bodyHtml:
A chance social media encounter has led to the race-against-time discovery of a new species of giant waterlily that has until now been hidden in the depths of Colombia’s jungle.

But the plant, which is so huge it is visible from space, is already considered critically endangered.

Giant waterlilies, which can measure up to three metres across and carry the weight of a small child, are one of the oldest flowering plants in the world still alive today. They existed before the continents split apart and are present throughout culture, from the Egyptians to Monet.

Three years ago, while scrolling through Instagram, Carlos Magdalena, a world-renowned waterlily expert at the Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew, came across a photo of someone swimming among several giant waterlilies in the Inírida River in Guainía, Colombia.

Jeremiah Harris, who took the photo and who runs a carnivorous plant nursery in the US, was not aware of its significance, having mistakenly identified the waterlily as the more common Victoria amazonica.

However, when Magdalena saw the photo, he “immediately suspected” something was unusual as the natural range of the Victoria amazonica does not extend to the Inírida River.

He messaged Harris to track down the exact location and spent several years analysing satellite imagery and securing the funds and necessary permits to allow him to verify the presence of the waterlily for himself.

Along with a team from the Jardín Botánico in Bogotá and members of the local indigenous reserves, Magdalena went on a five-day expedition deep into the rainforest.

They spent several days exploring the flooded jungle with no luck, until, at the last moment, their driver advised them where to look. With only 10 hours left until their return flight, the team sailed overnight in total darkness to a small lake deep in the flooded rainforest, where they located a population of the waterlilies.

‘It was so emotional I shed a tear, it was one of those moments that will remain with me for life,’ Magdalena said. ‘Coming across something like this is absolutely totally fascinating, it’s jaw dropping.

‘Giant waterlilies give away their secrets slowly,’ he said. ‘It’s remarkable. We believe we know everything but the reality is we don’t, there’s lots of things still to be discovered and protected.’

The team collected the material needed to begin a formal identification, with a paper published on Friday in the journal Phytotaxa confirming it as a new species to science. The waterlily has been given the official name Victoria colombiana. There are just three other known giant waterlilies.

Related: Newly identified waterlily species is world’s largest

Harris, who is an author of the study, said his friends always teased him for taking selfies with plants, but the fact this one ended in the discovery of a new species was ‘incredible’.

‘I was just so excited, absolutely elated,’ he said.

Magdalena said: ‘This is one of those extraordinary stories where indigenous and horticultural knowledge with the help of social media and technology came together to uncover a truly extraordinary botanical achievement.’

The team estimates there are between 30 and 50 of the Victoria colombiana waterlilies in the wild, making them extremely rare and at risk of extinction.

Maarten Christenhusz, a plant taxonomist who analysed the sample, said new species were found all the time, but few were as ‘large, spectacular and emblematic as this one. This new giant waterlily can even be seen from space, which is a striking reminder of how much we still don’t know about life on our planet.’

The team is working towards an official International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) Red List designation.

Efforts are also under way to support the long-term conservation of the waterlily, including the possibility of establishing a naturalised population in a more accessible lake within indigenous territory. The researchers hope to continue efforts to collect the plant’s seed, with the aim of cultivating it in Bogotá. If these efforts are successful, there is a chance the waterlily may be grown at Kew Gardens.
output.standfirst: A photo shared on Instagram led researchers to Victoria colombiana, a newly identified giant waterlily visible from space that is already critically endangered, with only 30 to 50 known in the wild.
